item.title: “Monks, as long as the community of monks is not dominated by craving — that craving which leads to another state of existence — then,…
item.description:
“Monks, as long as the community of monks is not dominated by craving — that craving which leads to another state of existence — then, monks, the community of monks can be expected to prosper and not decline.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 16 – Mahāparinibbānasutta

item.title: “Monks, the bones of a single person, if collected and preserved without being destroyed, would form a heap of bones, a pile of bones, a…
item.description:
“Monks, the bones of a single person, if collected and preserved without being destroyed, would form a heap of bones, a pile of bones, a mass of bones as great as this Mount Vepulla.

The bones of a single person
Accumulated in one lifetime
Would be a heap like a mountain —
So said the Great Sage.

This great mountain of bones
Is called Vepulla,
North of Vulture’s Peak
In the Magadhan hills.

But one who sees the Four Noble Truths
With perfect wisdom —
Suffering and its origin,
The transcending of suffering,
The Noble Eightfold Path
Leading to suffering’s stilling —

That person, wandering at most
Seven more times,
Makes an end of suffering,
Destroying all fetters.”

From: Itivuttaka 24
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, knowing form as impermanent … knowing feeling as impermanent … knowing perception as impermanent … knowing formations as impermanent … knowing consciousness as impermanent,…
item.description:
“Monks, knowing form as impermanent … knowing feeling as impermanent … knowing perception as impermanent … knowing formations as impermanent … knowing consciousness as impermanent, changing, fading, ceasing — he sees all consciousness, past and present, as impermanent, suffering, subject to change. Seeing thus with correct wisdom as it actually is, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are abandoned. Being abandoned, he does not become distressed. Not being distressed, he dwells at ease. Dwelling at ease, that monk is called ‘one who has stilled all signs and is wholly inclined toward Nibbāna.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.43
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by nature has strong lust, and he constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of lust. By nature he has strong ill-will, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of ill-will. By nature he has strong delusion, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of delusion. With pain and grief, with tearful face and crying, he lives the holy life that is fully complete and pure. At the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in this realm. This, monks, is called a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Monks, why is it called form? It is deformed (ruppati), monks, therefore it is called form. Deformed by what? Deformed by cold, deformed by heat,…
item.description:
“Monks, why is it called form? It is deformed (ruppati), monks, therefore it is called form. Deformed by what? Deformed by cold, deformed by heat, deformed by hunger, deformed by thirst, deformed by contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and serpents. It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called form. And why, monks, is it called feeling? It feels (vedeti), monks, therefore it is called feeling. What does it feel? It feels pleasure, it feels pain, it feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure. It feels, monks, therefore it is called feeling. And why, monks, is it called perception? It perceives (sañjānāti), monks, therefore it is called perception. What does it perceive? It perceives blue, it perceives yellow, it perceives red, it perceives white. It perceives, monks, therefore it is called perception.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.79

item.title: “Monks, the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as its end.…
item.description:
“Monks, the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as its end. For what reason is this said? When a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, his mind retreats, turns back, and draws away from sexual intercourse, and thus his mind is not strained, becomes peaceful, and disenchantment arises. Just as, monks, a cock’s feather or a sinew thrown into fire retreats, turns back, draws away, and is not strained — so too, when a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, his mind retreats, turns back, draws away from sexual intercourse, and thus his mind is not strained, becomes peaceful, and disenchantment arises. If a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, yet his mind still runs after, gets stuck in sexual intercourse, and disenchantment does not arise, then he should understand: ‘The perception of foulness is not developed in me; there is no distinction before and after in me; I have not attained the fruit of development.’ There he is clearly aware. If a monk dwells much with the perception of foulness, his mind retreats, turns back, draws away from sexual intercourse, his mind is not strained, becomes peaceful, and disenchantment arises, then he should understand: ‘The perception of foulness is developed in me; there is a distinction before and after in me; I have attained the fruit of development.’ There he is clearly aware. That the perception of foulness, when developed and cultivated, is of great fruit, great benefit, merging with the deathless, having the deathless as its end — for this reason it is said.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 7.49

item.title: “Dependent on attachment, this suffering arises. By the complete destruction of all attachments, suffering does not come to be. See the world with its multitude,…
item.description:
“Dependent on attachment, this suffering arises. By the complete destruction of all attachments, suffering does not come to be.

See the world with its multitude,
Overcome by ignorance,
Beings given to birth,
Delighting in becoming,
Not freed from existence.

For one who burns up existence,
At all times and places,
All this existence —
Impermanent, suffering, subject to change —

Seeing this as it really is
With perfect wisdom,
Craving for existence is abandoned,
As is the delight in non-existence.

With the complete destruction of craving,
Dispassion, cessation, complete,
That is Nibbāna.
That monk, cooled,
Without clinging to renewed existence,
Has conquered Māra,
Won the battle,
Crossed over all forms of existence.”

From: Udana 3.10
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?” “Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual…
item.description:
“Venerable sir, ‘stain’ is called a stain. What term is synonymous with what is called ‘stain’?”
“Venerable sir, evil, unwholesome states, the realm of sensual desire, are synonymous with what is called ‘stain.’”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 5 – Anaṅgaṇasutta

item.title: “Here, Udāyi, a person lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments. But while he lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments,…
item.description:
“Here, Udāyi, a person lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments. But while he lives aiming at the abandoning of attachments, the relinquishment of attachments, sometimes, from time to time, distorted thoughts, thoughts and considerations connected with attachments continue to arise. Udāyi, mindfulness arises slowly and he quickly abandons that thought, dispels it, ends it, destroys it. Udāyi, just as a man might drop two or three drops of water onto an iron pan that has been heated all day—slowly those drops fall, quickly they evaporate and vanish. Udāyi, I say: ‘This person is still bound, not freed.’ Why is that? Udāyi, the difference in his faculties has been fully understood by me.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 66 – Laṭukikopamasutta

item.title: “And, lord of gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does…
item.description:
“And, lord of gods, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk does not delight in those forms, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, that monk attains Nibbāna. There are sounds cognizable by the ear … odors … tastes … touches … Lord of gods, there are phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk does not delight in those phenomena, does not praise them, and dwells without lust for them — then, because he does not delight, does not praise, and dwells without lust, not depending on them, consciousness arises without clinging to them. Without clinging, lord of gods, that monk attains Nibbāna. This, lord of gods, is the cause, this is the reason why some beings here and now attain Nibbāna.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.118
